evidence: agents/orchestrator/main.py:683-692 — @app.get('/admin/killswitch') and @app.post('/admin/killswitch/athena') have ZERO auth: set_athena_kill() just does _kill_switches['athena_hunter']=bool(body.killed) with no header/token/cookie check. REACHABILITY IS THE CRUX AND IT IS BAD: docker-compose.agents.yml:6-7 publishes orchestrator as ports: '8001:8001' (binds 0.0.0.0 on the host), UNLIKE audit-monitor (expose: 8787, line 113) and web-server (expose: 3000, line 131) which are internal-only. nginx/nginx-ssl.conf has NO location for /admin or :8001 — verified live: `GET https://aing.bhnoc.com/admin/killswitch` -> 404 (not routed). BUT direct `GET http://aing.bhnoc.com:8001/admin/killswitch` returned HTTP 200 body {"athena_hunter":false} from my allow-listed IP over the public internet. So the orchestrator admin surface is exposed on the host's public interface, gated ONLY by the AWS security group — it is NOT confined to the docker network. Sweep 1's Bearer hardening on the audit-monitor proxy (tools/audit-monitor/app.py:418-424 _has_valid_bearer) is fully bypassable: hit :8001 directly. Note the proxy at app.py:404/427 forwards to the orchestrator WITHOUT any auth header, so the orchestrator was designed to trust its caller. This is a live unauth path (assuming SG lets an attacker reach 8001); the POST would silently force every athena_hunter query to the cover response = stealth full-platform DoS. I did NOT POST to any killswitch endpoint.
fix: Two-part: (1) In agents/orchestrator/main.py add a shared-secret gate on the state-changing route — read an env token (e.g. ADMIN_TOKEN) and require a matching Bearer header on POST /admin/killswitch/athena using secrets.compare_digest, returning 401 otherwise (mirror audit-monitor's _has_valid_bearer). (2) Make the audit-monitor proxy send that header: in tools/audit-monitor/app.py:427 add headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {ADMIN_TOKEN}'} to the client.post, and inject ADMIN_TOKEN into both services in docker-compose.agents.yml. Belt-and-suspenders: also change orchestrator ports to '127.0.0.1:8001:8001' (or drop the published port entirely and use expose:) so it is not on the public interface at all — nothing external needs :8001 since traffic flows nginx->web-server->orchestrator on the docker net.

evidence: scripts/redate_slice.py:74-94 clear_dst_partition() unconditionally glue.delete_partition(...PartitionValues=[DST_DT]) then paginates s3://blackhat-pope-parquet/<table>/dt=<DST_DT>/ and s3.delete_objects for every object found. main() (line 131-136) calls clear_dst_partition(t) at line 135 immediately BEFORE running the INSERT q(sql) at line 136, for every physical (non-VIRTUAL_VIEW) table returned by physical_tables(). No --dry-run, no confirmation prompt, no --yes guard; the only argv handling (line 124) is an optional table allow-list. DST_DT is hardcoded '2026-07-24' (line 24) = today. MITIGATING FACTS: the delete is scoped to the DESTINATION partition (dt=DST_DT), never the source SRC_DT=2026-04-24 (line 23) that the slice is derived from; the script's whole purpose (docstring lines 1-14) is to regenerate the re-datable demo slice into today's partition, so today's partition is expected to be disposable/synthetic. It targets the parquet data bucket blackhat-pope-parquet, not source telemetry. Real-data-loss scenario is narrow but real: if genuine (non-synthetic) data ever lands in dt=<today> for any table, running this wipes it irreversibly before re-inserting only the shifted 3h slice. This is an operator-run maintenance script, not in the request path — hence medium, not high.
fix: Add argparse with a required explicit --dst-dt (remove the silent 'today' default so a wrong/absent date can't fire), a --dry-run that lists the Glue partition + S3 keys that WOULD be deleted without deleting, and an interactive confirmation (or --yes) before the first destructive call. Optionally print the object count/prefix per table before delete. No app-code change needed; this is operator tooling.
